prompt: You run two replicas of a service behind a load balancer. Both replicas use plain print() statements for logging. What specifically breaks that structured JSON logging with a request_id field fixes?
choices: print() statements are slower to execute than logging calls
There is no way to correlate the log lines for a single request across the two separate, interleaved stdout streams
print() output cannot be captured by Docker at all
Python's print() function does not support string formatting

prompt: In the structured logging example, where does the request_id value come from for an incoming request?
choices: It is always a hardcoded constant set once at app startup
It is read from an X-Request-Id header if present, otherwise generated fresh with uuid4()
It is the process ID of the Python interpreter
It is read from the database row being queried

prompt: A container deployed on ECS Fargate writes JSON log lines to stdout. What additional code does the application need to write to get those lines into CloudWatch Logs?
choices: None — the awslogs log driver configured in the task definition ships stdout to CloudWatch automatically
The app must open a direct HTTPS connection to the CloudWatch Logs API for every log line
The app must install the CloudWatch agent binary inside its own process
The app must write logs to a file and then upload that file to S3 on a cron schedule

prompt: A /health endpoint is implemented as: `return "OK", 200` with no other logic. What failure mode does this fail to catch?
choices: It will crash the process immediately on any request
It always reports healthy even when the database the app depends on is completely unreachable
It returns 404 instead of 200
It cannot run inside a Docker container

prompt: Why does the improved /health endpoint use `connect_timeout=2` on the database connection attempt instead of letting it wait indefinitely?
choices: To make the endpoint's JSON response smaller
Postgres requires a timeout argument or it refuses the connection
So a hanging dependency check doesn't itself cause the health check to hang, which could make the platform treat an already-struggling instance even more unpredictably
To satisfy a Flask routing requirement

prompt: When the improved /health endpoint detects the database is unreachable, what HTTP status code should it return, and why?
choices: 200, because the endpoint itself still responded successfully
404, because the database row cannot be found
503, signaling the service is not ready to serve traffic, which ECS/Cloud Run can act on by stopping routing to that instance
500, because any failure should always be a generic server error

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend NOT logging an INFO-level line every time the health check endpoint is hit successfully?
choices: Flask does not allow logging inside endpoints bound to /health
The platform calls /health every ~30 seconds per instance, and logging each success would bury the signal you need during a real incident in noise
Successful health checks are not valid JSON
CloudWatch rejects log lines that occur more than once per minute

prompt: A CloudWatch Logs Insights query filters on `duration_ms > 1000` and `level = "WARN"`. What property of the application's logging is required for this query to work at all?
choices: The app must send logs directly to CloudWatch Logs Insights via a dedicated SDK call per query
The app must log plain text strings containing the word 'warning'
The app must emit structured JSON log lines with actual duration_ms and level fields, not free-text messages
The ECS task definition must set awslogs-stream-prefix to 'duration_ms'
